```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

The table functions (`sstable.baseline()`, `sstable.ae()`,
`sstable.survcomp()`, ...) return either a finished `flextable` or, with
`flextable = FALSE`, an *sstable*: a list with a character matrix `table`
and a `footer`. This vignette shows how to turn sstables into report tables,
how to edit them, and how to build a table of your own in the same style.

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ss_flextable()`, `ss_huxtable()` | render an sstable as a flextable or huxtable |
| `ft_sstheme()`, `ht_theme_kable()`, `ht_theme_markdown()` | apply the sstable look to any flextable or huxtable |
| `sstable.baseline.edit()` | adds the header and footer to a baseline table you edited |
| `ss_header()`, `ss_body()`, `ss_section()`, `ss_template()`, `ss_format()` | mark the rows of a hand-made table |
| `print()` | prints an sstable matrix in the console |

```{r}
library(C306)
```

The examples use `baseline_data`, a **simulated** two-arm trial bundled with
the package.

```{r}
bl <- baseline_data
bl$Arm <- factor(bl$Arm, levels = c("Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"))
tab <- sstable.baseline(age + sex + bmi + ablettscore ~ Arm, data = bl)
names(tab)
```

## Rendering: `ss_flextable()` and `ss_huxtable()`

`ss_flextable()` turns an sstable into a `flextable` with bold header rows,
indented row groups and striped body rows. `add_footer` appends notes to the
table's own footer:

```{r}
ss_flextable(tab, add_footer = "Data are simulated.")
```

Given only the matrix, it uses `footer` instead, and `bg` sets the colour of
the stripes:

```{r}
ss_flextable(tab$table, footer = "A custom footer", bg = "#E8F0F8")
```

`ss_huxtable()` does the same with the `huxtable` package, which also prints
to the console, LaTeX and Markdown. It needs `huxtable`, which is only
suggested by C306:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("huxtable", quietly = TRUE)}
ss_huxtable(tab, caption = "Baseline characteristics", caption_pos = "top")
```

## Theming any table

The same look can be applied to tables not made by C306. `ft_sstheme()`
themes a flextable:

```{r}
ft_sstheme(flextable::flextable(head(bl[, c("usubjid", "age", "sex", "Arm")])))
```

`ht_theme_markdown()` (stripes) and `ht_theme_kable()` (borders, like
`knitr::kable()`) theme a huxtable; `header_rows` says which rows are headers:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("huxtable", quietly = TRUE)}
ht <- huxtable::as_hux(head(bl[, c("usubjid", "age", "sex", "Arm")]))
ht_theme_markdown(ht, header_rows = 1)
ht_theme_kable(ht, header_rows = 1)
```

## Printing in the console

An sstable matrix prints as a plain matrix, or, with `huxtable` installed and
`pretty = TRUE` (the default, set by `options(ss_pretty.print = )`), as a
formatted text table:

```{r}
print(tab$table, pretty = FALSE)
```

## Editing a baseline table: `sstable.baseline.edit()`

To change the content of a baseline table before it is formatted, ask for the
raw matrix with `matrix.raw = TRUE`, edit its cells, and pass it back to
`sstable.baseline.edit()` with the same formula and data. It adds the header
rows and the footer (`footer` adds your own notes). Keep the first column as
it is: the function uses the variable names there to order the rows.

```{r}
raw <- sstable.baseline(age + sex ~ Arm, data = bl, matrix.raw = TRUE)
raw
raw[1, 3] <- paste0(raw[1, 3], "*")   # flag the age summary of the first arm
edited <- sstable.baseline.edit(raw, age + sex ~ Arm, data = bl,
                                footer = "* Illustrative flag added by hand.")
ss_flextable(edited)
```

To rename rows, set a `label` attribute on the variables before calling
`sstable.baseline()` instead, as shown in
`vignette("C306_vignette_v6", package = "C306")`.

## Building a table from scratch

Any character matrix can be rendered in the sstable style once its rows are
marked as header, section (a row-group title) or body rows. The functions
`ss_header()`, `ss_section()` and `ss_body()` do this one kind at a time:

```{r}
m <- rbind(c("", "Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"),
           c("Age, years", "50", "48"),
           c("Sex", "", ""),
           c("- Female", "30 (22%)", "29 (21%)"),
           c("- Male", "105 (78%)", "107 (79%)"))
m <- ss_header(m, 1)
m <- ss_body(m, c(2, 4, 5))
m <- ss_section(m, 3)
rownames(m)
ss_flextable(ss_format(m, .guess = FALSE))
```

`ss_format()` does it in one step. Give the rows of each kind, or let it
guess: header rows come first, a section row has text only in its first
column, and the rest are body rows. `template` (`"baseline"`, `"survcomp"`
or `"ae"`, also set with `ss_template()`) chooses the layout rules:

```{r}
m2 <- rbind(c("", "Sham procedure", "", "Intrathecal treatment", ""),
            c("Characteristic", "n", "Summary", "n", "Summary"),
            c("Age, years", "135", "50 (40-60)", "136", "48 (41-55)"),
            c("Sex", "", "", "", ""),
            c("- Female", "", "30 (22%)", "", "29 (21%)"))
f <- ss_format(m2)
rownames(f)
ss_flextable(f, footer = "Median (Q1-Q3) or n (%). Illustrative numbers.")
```

Tables made this way can be stacked with tables made by the package functions
and with each other; see `as_sstable()` in
`vignette("regression", package = "C306")` for assembling a table from header
and body parts.
